fixes.explanation: Right, because Daniel says no animal could stand against him. There was also no deliverance from his power. He did as he pleased, and that's the whole picture.
Nothing in the verse says the ram is afraid. He's the one doing the charging, and no animal could stand against him. Daniel says he did as he pleased and became great.
There's no staring contest in this vision. Daniel says the goat rushed at the ram with furious power. Then verse 7 says he struck the ram. Neither verse has the goat stopping short.
That's what Daniel sees. The goat “…threw him to the ground and trampled him…” The ram was powerless to stand against him. The same ram that did as he pleased is now thrown down and trampled.
Nothing in this verse shrinks. Daniel says the horn flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did. Back in verse 9, he says it emerged as a little horn and grew extensively.
Gabriel doesn't say the vision is about Daniel's own future. He says the vision concerns the time of the end. Daniel's own life isn't what Gabriel names.

Yes. Gabriel says these are four kingdoms that will rise from that nation, “…but will not have the same power.” So four kingdoms replace the broken horn. Gabriel says they will not have the same power.
This statement is true, friend. Gabriel says the four kingdoms will rise from that nation but “…will not have the same power.” The verse says exactly that, so the statement stands.
That's right. Gabriel says, “His power will be great, but it will not be his own.” Great power, but not his own. I won't guess whose it is, because the verse doesn't say.
Gabriel doesn't say the king keeps ruling until old age. He says the king will be broken off. His words are, “Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.”

The king isn't in this verse at all, so nobody here is deciding whether to believe it. Gabriel says, “Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.” That's the whole reason, and it's about time, not about who's convinced.
That's what Daniel says. “Then I got up and went about the king’s business.” Sick days end and the work doesn't. He goes back to it after the vision and the days he lay ill.
